headline: Massachusetts leads national women’s and children’s health ranking as New England fills top five
dek: Massachusetts ranked first in the new America’s Health Rankings report, with Vermont, New Hampshire and Connecticut also landing among the five strongest states. The report praises regional strengths while warning that maternal health, mental health and access gaps remain.
body: Massachusetts ranked No. 1 nationally for the health of women and children in a new report released Wednesday, and the result came with an unusually strong regional pattern: Vermont ranked No. 2, New Hampshire No. 3 and Connecticut No. 5. Minnesota was the only state outside New England in the top five.

The 2026 Health of Women and Children Report from [America’s Health Rankings](https://www.americashealthrankings.org/publications/reports/2026-health-of-women-and-children-report/state-rankings) evaluates 83 measures in five categories: social and economic factors, physical environment, behaviors, clinical care and health outcomes. Massachusetts ranked first overall for the second consecutive year and also ranked first in the report’s separate women’s and children’s health comparisons. The Massachusetts administration said the state’s figures in the report largely draw on data through 2024, while individual measures use different reporting periods.

The regional concentration is more than a one-year snapshot. America’s Health Rankings says Massachusetts, Vermont, New Hampshire, Minnesota and Connecticut have all remained in the report’s top 10 since the first edition in 2016. The organization cautions that the rankings are a composite measure, so they describe broad conditions across states rather than the experience of every family, town or medical service area.

Massachusetts’ strongest results included a low infant-mortality rate, a low prevalence of obesity among women and a high rate of food sufficiency among children. The report also identified a teen suicide rate of 4.6 deaths per 100,000 adolescents ages 15 to 19, the lowest rate in the country in the comparison. Massachusetts had 224.2 pediatricians per 100,000 people ages 0 to 21 in September 2025, another national high cited in the report.

The state’s category scores help explain why it led the overall table. Massachusetts ranked No. 1 in social and economic factors, No. 2 in clinical care, No. 3 in health outcomes and No. 4 in behaviors. Its weakest category was physical environment, where it ranked No. 13. The report’s measures cover conditions that shape health outside a doctor’s office, including family resources, preventive care and the environments where children grow up.

The report does not describe a clean bill of health. For Massachusetts, it lists adolescent illicit-drug use, cervical-cancer screening and the share of infants exclusively breastfed for six months among the state’s challenges. Nationally, the report found that maternal health outcomes worsened over the decade even as infant mortality, smoking during pregnancy and teen birth rates improved. It also found declines in children’s physical activity and access to care, along with growing mental-health concerns among women and children.

Those national trends give the regional ranking a practical policy question: how can strong statewide averages reach communities that have fewer providers or face higher barriers to care? The report says pediatricians have become more numerous overall but remain unevenly distributed, leaving many rural and underserved communities with fewer options. Its state-ranking site also provides disparity ratios for selected measures so readers can examine differences within states instead of treating a single rank as the whole story.

Massachusetts officials made a similar distinction in a [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/massachusetts-ranked-1-state-in-the-nation-for-womens-and-childrens-health) about the ranking. The Healey administration pointed to its 2024 maternal-health law, expanded postpartum home visiting and maternal mental-health programs, and updates to postpartum screening requirements. At the same time, the administration acknowledged that racial, ethnic, geographic and income disparities remain and said the ranking should be treated as a reason to continue the work rather than as proof that every family has equal access.

For New England readers, the top-five cluster offers both a regional strength and a test. Vermont, New Hampshire and Connecticut share the report’s favorable national position with Massachusetts, but the report’s measures show that the region still has to address mental health, affordability, provider distribution and unequal outcomes. The next step is less about defending a ranking than tracking whether those gaps narrow in the data that follow.
